query: In Lewis et al. (2020), what is the difference between the RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token formulations, and how many retrieved documents does each marginalise over?
reference_answer: RAG-Sequence treats the retrieved document as a single latent variable and uses the same retrieved document to generate the complete sequence. RAG-Token instead draws a different latent document for each target token, so the generator can choose content from several documents. In both models the top K documents are retrieved by the retriever and the generator probabilities are marginalised over them.

query: Which Wikipedia dump, chunk size, index size and index implementation did Lewis et al. (2020) use for their non-parametric memory?
reference_answer: They used the December 2018 Wikipedia dump, split each article into disjoint 100-word chunks for a total of 21M documents, and built a single MIPS index with FAISS using a Hierarchical Navigable Small World approximation.

query: How do Lewis et al. (2020) fine-tune the retriever and generator together, and which sub-model is deliberately left frozen?
reference_answer: They jointly train the retriever and generator components without any direct supervision on which document should be retrieved, minimising the negative marginal log-likelihood of each target with Adam. Updating the document encoder BERT is costly because it requires the index to be refreshed, so they keep the document encoder and index fixed and fine-tune only the query encoder BERT and the BART generator.

query: Lewis et al. (2020) name two approximations for decoding RAG-Sequence. What are they called and what distinguishes them?
reference_answer: For RAG-Sequence the likelihood does not break into a conventional per-token likelihood, so a single beam search cannot solve it; beam search is run per document and scoring each hypothesis gives the procedure they call ThoroughDecoding. For longer output sequences that require many extra forward passes, they approximate the probability of hypotheses not generated for a document as zero, which they call FastDecoding.

query: In Lewis et al. (2020), which parts of the RAG system are called parametric memory and non-parametric memory, and what are the models behind each?
reference_answer: The generator parameters theta are called the parametric memory; they are BART-large, a pre-trained seq2seq transformer with 400M parameters, and the retrieved content is concatenated onto the input. The document index is called the non-parametric memory; it is built by a DPR bi-encoder retriever initialised from BERT, whose document index serves as the non-parametric memory.

query: Which two question-answering datasets was the DPR retriever used by Lewis et al. (2020) originally trained to retrieve documents for?
reference_answer: The retriever was trained to retrieve documents containing answers to TriviaQA questions and to NaturalQuestions questions.

query: What does Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) mean by the Probabilistic Relevance Framework, and which two ranking functions does it yield?
reference_answer: The Probabilistic Relevance Framework is a formal framework for document retrieval grounded in work done in the 1970s to 1980s, which led to the development of BM25. Later work in the PRF yielded retrieval models that can take document meta-data such as structure and link-graph information into account, producing BM25F.

query: State the Probability Ranking Principle as Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) give it, and how far does it hold?
reference_answer: If retrieved documents are ordered by decreasing probability of relevance on the data available, then the system's effectiveness is the best that can be obtained for the data. This is the Probability Ranking Principle, taken from [52] and an abbreviated version of the one in [40]. It can be justified under some further assumptions for a range of effectiveness measures, but it is not completely general because counter-examples can be constructed; those counter-examples depend on probabilities defined over a population of users, whereas the PRP is safe for the case considered, an individual user.

query: How does Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) argue that eliteness should be treated across BM25F's multiple document streams?
reference_answer: Applying the ranking function separately to each stream and then taking a linear combination would, in eliteness terms, assume a separate eliteness property for each term/stream pair and would need the usual independence assumptions between those distinct eliteness properties for the same term, which seems unreasonable. The better assumption is that eliteness is a term/document property shared across the streams of the document.

query: What two assumptions does Robertson and Zaragoza (2009) make before integrating non-textual relevance features into the PRF and BM25?
reference_answer: First they make the usual assumption of feature independence with respect to relevance odds. Second they assume that all non-textual features provide relevance information which is independent of the query. Under those two assumptions non-textual features integrate very easily into the PRF and BM25 scoring frameworks; taking the log shows that adding non-textual features simply adds a new term to the sum.

query: How was the value of learning the retrieval component tested, and on which task did the sparse lexical baseline come out best?
reference_answer: Two ablations were run: the retriever was frozen during training, and the dense retriever was replaced by a fixed BM25 system whose retrieval scores were used as the logits for the document distribution. Learned retrieval improved results on every task. BM25 was best on fact verification, presumably because those claims are heavily entity-centric and suit word-overlap retrieval; the gains from differentiable retrieval were largest on open-domain QA, where they are described as crucial.

query: Which corpus supplies both the training and the retrieval data, how is it tokenised, and how large is the retrieval database used at evaluation time?
reference_answer: Both roles go to a multilingual version of MassiveText, which totals over 5 trillion tokens from multiple sources and languages. It is tokenised with SentencePiece using a vocabulary of 128,000 tokens. During training the model retrieves from 600B tokens; at evaluation the database is the full union of the datasets, with books sub-sampled to 4%, giving an evaluation retrieval database of 1.75T tokens.

query: How is the key-value retrieval memory laid out, and what search implementation and latency are reported for querying it?
reference_answer: Each value is a pair of contiguous token chunks: the neighbour chunk used to compute the key and its continuation in the original document. The key is the BERT embedding of the neighbour chunk averaged over time. Both chunks have length 64, so each retrieved value has shape k x 128. Approximate nearest neighbours are queried in O(log T) time with the SCaNN library, which allows the 2 trillion token database to be queried in 10ms while evaluating or sampling.

query: Why are the retrieval keys produced by a frozen encoder rather than by a trained retriever?
reference_answer: The method builds a key-value database in which values store raw token chunks and keys are frozen BERT embeddings. A frozen model is used deliberately to avoid having to periodically re-compute embeddings over the entire database during training. Because the embedding operator is frozen, all approximate nearest neighbours can be precomputed and saved as part of the data, which is why on-the-fly retrieval is too slow to keep up with training.

query: How can an already pre-trained transformer be given a retrieval pathway cheaply, and what does that cost in extra weights and training?
reference_answer: Baseline models are extended by freezing the pre-trained weights and training only the chunked cross-attention and neighbour encoder parameters, which is under 10% of the weights for the 7B model. This requires only 6 million sequences, about 3% of the pre-training sequences. Because only the new weights are trained, evaluating the model without retrieval preserves the original performance exactly, and fine-tuning this way quickly surpasses the baseline and comes close to a model trained from scratch.

query: How is evaluation-time overlap between test and training data measured and filtered, and what does the analysis conclude about how much of the gain is leakage?
reference_answer: Evaluation sequences are split into chunks of at most 64 tokens; for each chunk the 10 closest training neighbours of length up to 128 are retrieved and the longest common token substring is computed, giving an overlap ratio from 0 to 1. Filtered bits-per-byte is then reported over chunks below a given overlap threshold. On the leaky corpora the slope is negative for both baselines and retrieval models, and the retrieval model exploits leakage more strongly, but retrieval still beats the baseline at every leakage level down to 12.5%, i.e. chunks sharing fewer than 8 contiguous tokens with their closest training chunk.

query: Why might a document be longer than average, and what does each of the two explanations imply for length normalisation in the ranking function?
reference_answer: Two extreme explanations are postulated. Under Verbosity some authors are simply more verbose than others, using more words to say the same thing, and this hypothesis suggests simply normalising observed term frequencies by dividing by document length. Under Scope some authors have more to say, writing a single document covering more ground, an extreme version being two or more documents concatenated, and this at least in its extreme form suggests the opposite. In a real collection the variation is due to either effect or to a combination, so the paper concludes that some kind of soft normalisation should be applied.

query: Why does the probabilistic relevance framework largely disregard where in a document a query term occurs, and what goes wrong if you try to build a model that does not?
reference_answer: For the most part the framework ignores positional information: it cares only about the number of occurrences of a term, not their position. Two reasons are given. It is extremely hard to develop a sound formal model of relevance that takes positional information into account without exploding the number of parameters, and position information has been shown to have surprisingly little effect on retrieval accuracy on average. Concretely, the natural way to consider positions is to characterise all sequences of query terms separated by some number of non-query terms, which leads to an excessively high-dimensional space that is very hard to factorise appropriately.

The term saturation is used for this behaviour: any one term's contribution to the document score cannot exceed a saturation point, the asymptotic limit, however frequently it occurs in the document.

query: In the two-Poisson treatment of term weighting, how is the estimation problem reduced to two cases, and what does the decomposition pattern express?
reference_answer: A random variable E called Eliteness is introduced that can take two values, elite and not elite. All the probabilities wanted are then decomposed over these two disjoint events, following the pattern P(alpha given beta) equals P(alpha given elite) times P(elite given beta) plus the not-elite counterpart. The relationship between eliteness and relevance is then written as p := P(E = elite|rel), with separate symbols for the relevant and the non-relevant case, and likewise term frequencies are related to eliteness.

query: How is term frequency turned into a variable in the Binary Independence Model, and why is the straightforward maximum-likelihood ratio rejected as the estimate to plug into the weight?
reference_answer: Term frequency TFi is treated as a binary variable with only the values zero and one, read without loss of generality as presence or absence of the term. The standard maximum likelihood estimate of a probability from trials is a simple ratio, but that is not a good estimator to plug into the weighting formula: the combination of a ratio of probabilities and a log function may yield positive or negative infinities as estimates. There are also good theoretical reasons to modify the simple ratio somewhat, to obtain a more robust estimator that introduces a small pseudo-count of frequency.

query: Which two open-domain question-answering benchmarks are used to evaluate the unsupervised retriever, which versions of them, and which Wikipedia snapshot serves as the retrieval collection?
reference_answer: The model is evaluated on NaturalQuestions and TriviaQA, using the open domain versions of both as introduced by Lee et al. (2019). For both datasets the collection to retrieve from is the English Wikipedia dump from Dec. 20, 2018. The reported metric is the number of questions for which at least one of the top-k passages contains the answer.

query: Why do the authors conclude that sampling two independent random crops is a better way to build positive pairs for a retriever than the inverse cloze task?
reference_answer: They report that the random cropping strategy outperforms the inverse cloze task in their setting. The explanation is distributional: because both views of a cropped pair are drawn from the same distribution, keys and queries have identical distributions, which leads to more stable training with MoCo than ICT does.

query: In the queue-based negative sampling scheme, what is the name given to the slowly updated key network, and how are its parameters kept in step with the query network?
reference_answer: The queue-based scheme is called MoCo and it keeps two networks: one for the keys, parametrized by theta_k, and one for the query, parametrized by theta_q. The query network is updated by backpropagation and stochastic gradient descent, while the key network, or Momentum encoder, is updated from the parameters of the query network using an exponential moving average.

query: What MoCo queue size, momentum, temperature, document length and span-size range are used for the contrastive pre-training of the retriever?
reference_answer: Pre-training uses the MoCo algorithm with a queue of size 131,072, a momentum value of 0.9995 and a temperature of 0.05. The random cropping augmentation uses documents of 256 tokens with span sizes sampled between 5% and 50% of the document length, and token deletion is applied with a probability of 10%.

query: On the zero-shot benchmark, how many of the evaluation datasets does the fully unsupervised model beat BM25 on for recall@100, and which two datasets hold it back?
reference_answer: The unsupervised model is better than BM25 on 11 out of 15 datasets from the benchmark for the recall@100, but BM25 largely outperforms it on two datasets with specific features: Trec-COVID, whose training data was collected before the COVID outbreak, and Touche-2020, which contains long documents that dense neural retrievers do not support well even after supervised training.

query: Why do the authors encode queries and documents with a single shared encoder rather than two, and which pre-trained architecture is that encoder initialised from?
reference_answer: They use a bi-encoder architecture in which documents and queries are encoded independently and the relevance score is the dot product of the two representations. Empirically they found that using the same encoder for both sides, as in Xiong et al. and Reimers & Gurevych, generally improves robustness for zero-shot transfer or few-shot learning and has no impact on other settings, unlike the two-encoder DPR arrangement. The shared encoder is initialised from BERT base uncased.

query: What term does the paper give to the practice of padding a short query with mask tokens, and what is that operation said to do?
reference_answer: Padding a short query with BERT's special mask tokens is called query augmentation. It lets BERT produce query-based embeddings at the positions corresponding to those masks, and serves as a soft, differentiable mechanism for learning to expand queries with new terms or to re-weigh existing terms according to their importance for matching the query.

query: Which faiss index does the end-to-end retrieval implementation use, and what example values does it give for the number of cells and for the number of partitions actually probed at search time?
reference_answer: The implementation uses an IVFPQ index, an inverted file with product quantization. It partitions the embedding space into P cells, e.g. P = 1000, by k-means clustering and assigns each document embedding to its nearest cell under the selected vector-similarity metric; when serving a query it searches only the nearest p partitions, e.g. p = 10.

query: What GPU, GPU memory, CPU and system RAM does the machine used to measure the reported re-ranking latencies have?
reference_answer: Re-ranking latency is measured on a server with a single Tesla V100 GPU with 32 GiB of memory, two Intel Xeon Gold 6132 CPUs, each with 14 physical cores and 24 hyperthreads, and 469 GiBs of RAM.

query: Why is a per-term maximum-similarity matching operation well suited to pruning, and what does that allow at retrieval time?
reference_answer: A summation of maximum similarity computations stands out as a particularly cheap interaction mechanism, and more importantly it is amenable to highly efficient pruning for top-k retrieval. which lets the system use vector-similarity algorithms for skipping documents without materialising the full interaction matrix.

query: How many passages does the MS MARCO Ranking collection contain, where were they gathered from, and which metric does its official evaluation use?
reference_answer: MS MARCO is a collection of 8.8M passages from web pages, which were gathered from Bing's results, paired with 1M real-world queries. The official evaluation metric is MRR@10.

query: When the late-interaction model is fitted, which parameters are fine-tuned, which are trained from scratch, which part of it has no trainable parameters at all, and what optimizer is used?
reference_answer: The model is differentiable end-to-end: the BERT encoders are fine-tuned, while the additional parameters -- the linear layer and the embeddings of the [Q] and [D] markers -- are trained from scratch, and the Adam optimizer is used. The interaction mechanism itself has no trainable parameters; training uses a pairwise softmax cross-entropy loss over the computed scores of a positive and a negative document.

query: Which token's vector does the re-ranker feed to its classification layer to turn a scored pair into a relevance probability, and what size of model is used?
reference_answer: A BERT model LARGE is used as a binary classification model: the [CLS] vector is fed as input to a single layer neural network, which outputs the probability that the passage is relevant. That probability is computed for each passage independently, and the final list of passages is obtained by ranking them with respect to it.

query: In the paper's account of a question-answering pipeline, which stage is the re-ranker, what does the stage before it do, and what consumes its output?
reference_answer: A simple question-answering pipeline has three main stages. The first retrieves a large number, for example a thousand, of possibly relevant documents from a corpus by a standard mechanism such as BM25. The second is passage re-ranking, where each of those documents is scored and re-ranked by a more computationally intensive method. Finally the top ten or fifty re-ranked documents become the source of candidate answers for an answer generation module.

query: How large is the MS MARCO development set used for re-ranking, and why do some of its queries have no relevant passage at all?
reference_answer: The development set contains approximately 6,900 queries, each paired with the top 1,000 passages retrieved with BM25 from the MS MARCO corpus, and on average each query has one relevant passage. Some have none because the corpus was initially constructed by retrieving the top-10 passages from the Bing search engine and only then annotating them, so genuinely relevant passages may fall outside what BM25 retrieves.

query: Why does the paper decline to score TREC-CAR with the manual relevance judgements released for the test set, and what does it use instead?
reference_answer: The TREC-CAR 2017 organisers provide manual annotations for the test set, but only the top five passages retrieved by the systems submitted to the competition are manually annotated, so true relevant passages are not annotated when they rank low. The paper therefore evaluates with the automatic annotations, which provide relevance scores for all possible query-passage pairs.

query: What leakage risk does pre-training the re-ranker on an off-the-shelf BERT model create for the TREC-CAR evaluation, and how is the risk removed?
reference_answer: The official pre-trained BERT models were pre-trained on the full Wikipedia and have therefore already seen, in an unsupervised way, the Wikipedia documents used in the TREC-CAR test set. To avoid leaking test data into training, the BERT re-ranker was pre-trained only on the half of Wikipedia used by the training split of TREC-CAR.

query: What accelerator, batch size, schedule and learning rate are used to fine-tune the re-ranker on MS MARCO, and how much of the available training data does that consume?
reference_answer: The model is fine-tuned on a TPU v3-81 with a batch size of 128, that is 128 sequences of 512 tokens or 65,536 tokens per batch, for 100k iterations, which takes approximately 30 hours. That corresponds to 12.8M query-passage pairs, less than 2% of the full training set. Training uses ADAM with an initial learning rate of 3 × 10−6, beta 0.9 and 1-beta 0.999, L2 weight decay 0.01, warmup over the first 10,000 steps and then linear decay, plus a dropout probability of 0.1 on all layers.

query: A self-reflective retrieval-augmented generator widens its output vocabulary with two families of special tokens. What are those two families called, and which three groups does the second one split into?
reference_answer: The original vocabulary is expanded with two families of reflection tokens, named Critique and Retrieve. The Critique family is scored in three groups, which the paper's equations write as ISREL, ISSUP and ISUSE: whether a retrieved passage is relevant, whether a generated segment is supported by it, and whether the whole response is useful.

query: In the self-reflective RAG setup, which retriever is used by default, how many documents does it pull per input during training, and what retrieval threshold is set at inference for ordinary tasks versus the long-form citation task?
reference_answer: The default retriever is off-the-shelf Contriever-MS MARCO. During training it retrieves up to ten documents for each input; at inference the default context is the top five documents from the same retriever. The retrieval threshold is set to 0.2 for most tasks and to 0 for ALCE, because of the citation requirements there.

query: Retrieval in a self-reflective RAG system can be left to the model's own decision or handed to a probability threshold. How is that threshold defined, and what does raising it cost on the two short-form QA benchmarks?
reference_answer: Instead of relying only on the model's predicted retrieval token, a threshold can be set: retrieval fires when the probability of generating the retrieval token, normalized over the output tokens, surpasses it. A larger threshold means less retrieval. The measured accuracy degradation from retrieving less is smaller on PubHealth and larger on PopQA, while the retrieval frequency changes dramatically on both datasets as the threshold varies.

query: How large is the instruction-output training set used by the self-reflective framework, and which smaller subsets are drawn from it for the data-scaling analysis?
reference_answer: The framework trains on 150k instruction-output pairs. For the data-scaling analysis it randomly samples 5k, 10k, 20k and 50k instances from that original pool and fine-tunes four SELF-RAG variants on those subsets, comparing them to the model trained on the full 150k.

query: Why is producing reflection-token supervision described as cheaper than an RLHF-style pipeline, and what happens to the need for a separate critic at inference time?
reference_answer: Where an RLHF pipeline keeps separate reward models during training, here the critique is computed offline and inserted directly into the training corpus, and the generator is then trained with a standard LM objective, which significantly reduces training cost. Because the critic's predictions are baked into the corpus, the final generator learns to emit the reflection tokens itself and no longer relies on the critic at inference time.

query: Which base language models back the generator in this self-reflective approach, and which one is used to initialise the critic?
reference_answer: The generator is built on Llama2 at two sizes, 7B and 13B. The critic is initialised from Llama2 7B.

query: A corrective RAG pipeline scores every retrieved document and maps that score onto one of three actions. What are the three actions called and how are the boundaries between them set?
reference_answer: Three actions are defined: Correct, Incorrect, and the intermediate Ambiguous. A document above the upper threshold is treated as Correct, one below the lower threshold as Incorrect, and anything in between as Ambiguous. At the query level a retrieval counts as Correct if at least one document exceeds the upper threshold, and as Incorrect only when all retrieved documents are below the lower threshold.

query: What model is fine-tuned to act as the retrieval evaluator in this corrective pipeline, how many parameters does it have, and how many documents does it score per question?
reference_answer: The evaluator is initialised from T5-large and fine-tuned. At 0.77B parameters it is described as lightweight compared with the current LLMs, and it is contrasted with the instruction-tuned LLaMA-2 (7B) critic that tracks retrieval quality in Self-RAG. For every question the evaluator scores each of the generally 10 documents that were retrieved, with the question concatenated to each single document as input.

query: How did the authors show that the gains come from the corrective mechanism itself rather than from the extra web-search knowledge?
reference_answer: They gave RAG and Self-RAG the same web-search knowledge, so every system had access to the same scope of retrieved knowledge, and then compared against the corrective variants. Web search alone improved the baselines in most cases, but RAG augmented with the proposed self-correction mechanism outperformed the models consistently supplemented with web search knowledge in all cases, so the advancements are attributed primarily to the self-correction mechanism rather than to the supplementary web information. The stated corollary is that the retrieved context has to be enhanced with additional information.

query: How accurate is the lightweight retrieval evaluator on PopQA, compared with the prompted commercial LLM variants?
reference_answer: On PopQA the T5-based retrieval evaluator reaches 84.3, above plain ChatGPT at 58.0, ChatGPT-CoT at 62.4 and ChatGPT-few-shot at 64.7. The authors report that the lightweight T5-based evaluator significantly outperformed the competitive ChatGPT in all settings.

query: An adaptive retrieval-augmented QA system first classifies each query's complexity. How many levels does the classifier distinguish, and which answering strategy does each level select?
reference_answer: Three. 'A' marks a straightforward query that the LLM alone can answer; 'B' marks a query of moderate complexity that needs at least a single-step approach; 'C' marks a complex query requiring the most extensive multi-step solution.

query: The experimental comparison sorts competing systems into three difficulty tiers. What are the tiers called and which methods sit in each?
reference_answer: The tiers are Simple, Adaptive and Complex. Simple holds No Retrieval and the Single-step Approach. Adaptive holds Adaptive Retrieval, Self-RAG and the paper's own Adaptive-RAG. Complex is the Multi-step Approach, implemented with the state-of-the-art method that iteratively accesses both the retriever and the LLM with Chain-of-Thought reasoning. An Adaptive-RAG with an oracle classifier is reported separately as the ideal scenario.

query: No annotated dataset of query-complexity pairs exists for this setting, so where does the supervision for the complexity classifier come from?
reference_answer: It is constructed automatically, with no human-annotated complexity data involved. The datasets' own inductive bias supplies the fallback: the three retrieval-augmented strategies sometimes all fail on a query, leaving it unlabelled by outcome, so queries left over in single-hop datasets are labelled 'B' and those in multi-hop datasets 'C'. The classifier is then trained on these automatically collected query-complexity pairs with a cross-entropy loss, and is implemented as a T5-Large model.

query: The confusion matrix reported for the query-complexity classifier shows which class pairs it actually confuses, and at what rates?
reference_answer: 'C (Multi)' is sometimes misclassified as 'B (One)', at about 31%, and 'B (One)' as 'C (Multi)', at about 23%. 'A (No)' is the most confused: it is misclassified as 'B (One)' about 47% of the time and as 'C (Multi)' about 22% of the time. Despite these confusions the classifier still separates the three labels overall, and separates granularity levels that include not retrieving, retrieving once and retrieving repeatedly.

query: Why is labelling the query-complexity classifier from the datasets' inductive bias alone insufficient, and what does the training-strategy ablation show?
reference_answer: Bias-derived labels assume single-hop means one-step and multi-hop means multi-step, so they never cover the case where no documents are needed at all, and the authors note that existing datasets do not capture whether retrieval is required. Adding outcome-derived labels fixes this. The ablation reports, for the full strategy, 46.94 F1 with 1084 in the Step column, against 43.43 F1 with 640 for the bias-only variant 'w/oBinary', and 48.79 F1 with 1464 for the outcome-only variant 'w/oSilver', which scores 0.00 on the 'No' class. So the outcome-only silver labels are not optimal because they do not cover complexity labels over incorrectly predicted queries, which lowers generalization.

query: In a probabilistic term-weighting scheme the contribution of a query term grows with its frequency in the document but eventually flattens out, whereas a learned sparse ranker reads the importance of each vocabulary item straight off a pretrained language model. For each of the two systems, state where the weight attached to a term actually comes from, and say which component is responsible for producing it.
reference_answer: BM25 derives each term's weight inside the probabilistic framework: the observed term frequency is passed through a one-parameter saturation function fitted to the shape of the 2-Poisson mixture, so the weight increases monotonically with tf but is asymptotically bounded, and it is combined with an RSJ/IDF component. SPLADE instead reads the weight of a vocabulary item off a masked language model: term importance over the 30522-entry BERT WordPiece vocabulary is taken from the logit output distribution of the MLM layer.

query: Suppose the words of a query do not literally occur in the documents you want to rank. Describe, for the classical probabilistic ranker and for the learned sparse ranker, what mechanism exists to bridge that gap and what it costs.
reference_answer: The probabilistic ranker has no built-in bridge: a weight is applied only to terms present in the document, which fits the sparseness of the document-term matrix and inverted-index implementation, so bridging the gap is left to pseudo-relevance feedback - and the paper notes that this kind of expansion is likely to introduce synonyms or closely related words and may therefore worsen the term independence assumption. The learned sparse model bridges the gap inside the representation itself, motivated by the vocabulary mismatch problem, or, in its document-only variant, drops query expansion and query term weighting altogether so the ranking score depends only on document term weights, which can then be pre-computed offline and inference cost is reduced.

query: Two dense passage retrievers both produce one vector per query and one per document and score them with an inner product, yet one needs labelled question-passage data and the other is trained on raw text. For each, state what supplies the positive examples during training and where the negative examples come from.
reference_answer: The discriminatively trained retriever takes its positives from annotated QA data - the highest-ranked BM25 passage that contains the answer - and its negatives from three sources: random passages, BM25 passages that do not contain the answer but match most question tokens, and gold passages paired with other questions in the training set; its best configuration re-uses gold passages from the same mini-batch plus one BM25 negative. The contrastively trained retriever needs no labels: positive pairs are two views of the same text and negatives come from in-batch views or from a MoCo queue of representations from previous batches, trained with an InfoNCE loss.

query: Neither of these two retrievers is guaranteed to transfer to an unseen collection. For each, state what it claims about its behaviour outside its training domain relative to a plain term-frequency lexical baseline, and note the dataset on which the comparison is reported to be misleading.
reference_answer: The supervised dense retriever reports that it performs consistently better than BM25 on all of its evaluated datasets with a large gap at small k, and that a retriever trained on only 1,000 examples already outperforms BM25; but it flags SQuAD as the exception where BM25 has a clear advantage, because annotators wrote questions after seeing the passage, giving high lexical overlap. The unsupervised contrastive retriever starts from the opposite observation - in the zero-shot setting dense retrievers are often outperformed by classical term-frequency methods that require no supervision - and then reports an unsupervised model outperforming BM25 on 11 of 15 BEIR datasets for Recall@100.

query: One of these two dense retrievers compresses a whole passage into a single fixed-size vector; the other keeps a separate vector for every token and matches them individually. For each, state how the relevance score is actually computed and what constraint the scoring function must satisfy.
reference_answer: The single-vector retriever computes similarity as the dot product of the question and passage embeddings and explicitly requires that the similarity function be decomposable, so that the representations of the collection of passages can be pre-computed; the encoder is two independent BERT networks and the [CLS] token is the output, so d = 768. The multi-vector retriever encodes query and document into two bags of fixed-size embeddings and computes relevance by a late interaction defined as a summation of maximum similarity (MaxSim) operators; the embeddings are L2-normalised so the dot product of any two embeddings becomes their cosine similarity.

query: Serving throughput depends on how much encoder work happens per candidate. For each of these two dense retrieval architectures, state what is computed at query time relative to what was pre-computed, and report the quantitative cost figures given.
reference_answer: The multi-vector late-interaction architecture isolates almost all computation between queries and documents so that document representations can be pre-computed offline; it feeds BERT only a single, much shorter sequence rather than k sequences of length |q|+|d|, and is reported as over 170x cheaper in latency and 13,900x in FLOPs. The single-vector dense passage retriever pre-computes embeddings for all passages and indexes them with FAISS in memory, achieving 995.0 questions per second returning top 100 passages per question against 23.7 questions per second per CPU thread for BM25/Lucene - but it pays at index time, since the time required for building an index for dense vectors is much longer and computing dense embeddings on 21-million passages is resource intensive.

query: A passage-re-ranking pipeline has a first stage that must run over the whole corpus and a second stage that only sees a shortlist. For each of the two scoring functions described here, state at which stage it runs and what it needs as input to produce a score.
reference_answer: The cross-encoder is explicitly a second-stage passage re-ranker: a standard mechanism such as BM25 first retrieves a large number of candidate passages, the second stage scores and re-ranks each of them, and only the top ten or fifty feed the answer generation module. It takes the query as sentence A and the passage as sentence B in a single BERT model and turns the [CLS] vector into the probability of the passage being relevant. The probabilistic ranking function instead runs as a first-stage scorer directly over an inverted index: a trick removes terms not present in the document from the equation, so only present terms need weighting and no score need be computed for documents containing no query terms.

query: Both of these rankers have free parameters that somebody has to set. For each, say where the settings come from and what the paper says about how much guidance it gives for choosing them.
reference_answer: The neural re-ranker's settings come from supervised fine-tuning: a TPU v3-81 with batch size 128, i.e. 128 sequences * 512 tokens = 65,536 tokens/batch, for 100k iterations taking about 30 hours, corresponding to 12.8M query-passage pairs or less than 2% of the full training set, with ADAM at initial learning rate 3e-6 and dropout 0.1; no improvement was seen from training for another 3 days. The probabilistic ranking function is explicit that the model provides no guidance on how its internal parameters should be set, which is regarded as a limitation, with only empirical studies suggesting ranges such as 0.5 < b < 0.8 and 1.2 < k < 2; and the survey of open source implementations notes that none of the systems provide support for parameter optimisation.

query: For a retrieval-augmented language model, the document index has to stay usable while the model is being trained. Across the three lines of work that attach a parametric generator to a large external corpus, describe what happens to the index during training: what is held fixed, what has to be rebuilt, and what can be computed once in advance because the retriever never changes.
reference_answer: The RAG line holds the index fixed: updating the document encoder BERT during training is costly because it requires the document index to be periodically updated, and it keeps the document encoder (and index) fixed, only fine-tuning the query encoder BERT and the BART generator. REALM trains the retriever jointly, so the search index over pre-computed document embeddings goes stale after every gradient update on the retriever parameters; its solution is to refresh the index by asynchronously re-embedding and re-indexing all documents every several hundred training steps, and it also adds an empty null document to the top k retrieved documents so credit goes to a consistent sink when no retrieval is necessary. Retro avoids the problem entirely by using a frozen model, so embeddings never have to be recomputed over the entire database during training and all approximate nearest neighbours can be precomputed and saved as part of the data.

query: A retrieval-augmented language model has to decide both what unit of text to look up and how retrieved text enters the prediction. Compare the unit of retrieval and the way retrieved documents are used in the RAG, REALM and Retro formulations.
reference_answer: RAG retrieves fixed 100-word chunks - each Wikipedia article is split into disjoint 100-word chunks to make 21M documents, indexed in a single MIPS index - and marginalises the top K retrieved documents at generation time, drawing one latent document for the whole sequence in RAG-Sequence or a different latent document per target token in RAG-Token. REALM also works over documents but marginalises during pre-training, approximating the sum over the whole knowledge corpus by summing over the top k documents with the highest probability, with the ordering of documents under that probability being the same as under the relevance score, which is an inner product, so MaximumInnerProductSearch can be used. Retro retrieves at the granularity of contiguous token chunks: an n = 2048 token sequence is split into l chunks of size m = 64, each chunk is augmented with a set of k nearest neighbours from the database, and each stored value consists of two contiguous chunks - the neighbour chunk used to compute the key and its continuation.

query: Three systems all decide whether or what to retrieve before answering. For each, state what the decision actually is, who or what makes it, and whether it is taken once per query or interleaved with generation.
reference_answer: Self-RAG takes the decision inside generation: the model decodes a retrieval token to evaluate the utility of retrieval, and if retrieval is not required it predicts the next output segment as a standard LM would; the tokens are produced by unifying the reflection tokens as next-token predictions from an expanded model vocabulary. CRAG separates the decision into a distinct lightweight component: a retrieval evaluator, initialised from T5-large and fine-tuned, estimates a relevance score per retrieved document which is quantified into a total of three confidence degrees - Correct, Incorrect and Ambiguous - and triggers the corresponding action. Adaptive-RAG takes the decision once per query, with a smaller LM classifier predicting the complexity level of incoming queries with automatically collected labels.

query: Each of these three approaches makes an explicit engineering trade-off between quality and cost, and each states that trade-off in a different currency. For each, state the currency and the concrete position the paper takes.
reference_answer: The probabilistic function argues in index efficiency: the verbosity hypothesis suggests simply normalising observed tfs by dividing by document length while the scope hypothesis suggests the opposite, and a combination of the two implies some kind of soft normalisation - and the derivation is built so that only terms present in a document need weighting, which is crucial for efficient implementation using inverted indices. Reciprocal rank fusion argues in training supervision and simplicity: unsupervised methods are attractive because they require no training examples, and its only free constant was found to be near-optimal without being critical. The learned sparse model argues in floating-point operations: a FLOPS regularizer is introduced as a smooth relaxation of the average number of floating-point operations necessary to compute the score between a query and a document, and its document-only variant makes everything pre-computable offline, reducing inference cost.

query: In Guu et al. (2020), how is REALM's pre-training and fine-tuning objective formalised, and into which two steps is the prediction probability decomposed?
reference_answer: The paper formalises both pre-training and fine-tuning tasks as a retrieve-then-predict generative process: the model takes an input x and learns a distribution p(y|x) over possible outputs y, and REALM decomposes p(y|x) into two steps, retrieve then predict.

query: How are the two embedding functions of the REALM retriever built from raw text, and which special tokens wrap the resulting input?
reference_answer: The embedding functions use BERT-style Transformers, and spans of text are joined by applying wordpiece tokenization, separating them with [SEP] tokens, prefixing a [CLS] token and appending a final [SEP] token.

query: In Guu et al. (2020), what does the word "document" actually denote, given that the knowledge corpus is a whole encyclopaedia?
reference_answer: The authors use the term document loosely to refer to a passage from the knowledge corpus, not necessarily a whole article.

query: When REALM pre-training is ablated by resetting one component to its baseline, what is learned by the retriever and what by the encoder?
reference_answer: Both the encoder and the retriever benefit from REALM training separately, but the best result requires both components acting in unison.

reference_answer: A parallel process re-embeds the corpus documents and rebuilds the MIPS index, giving one index refresh per approximately 500 training steps. The results suggest that a stale index can hurt model training, and further reducing this staleness could offer better optimization.

query: In the DPR end-to-end QA system, how does the reader choose which retrieved passage to answer from?
reference_answer: Given the top k retrieved passages, up to 100 in the experiments, the reader assigns a passage selection score to each passage and also extracts an answer span from each passage with its own span score. query: How many train and dev questions are in the NaturalQuestions split used to train the retriever, and what is the size of the corresponding test set?
reference_answer: Table 1 lists the NaturalQuestions counts as 79,168 train and 58,880 dev, with test columns of 8,757 and 3,610.

query: How is the hybrid BM25+DPR retriever constructed by Karpukhin et al. (2020), and what weight is given to the dense score?
reference_answer: Two initial sets of top-2000 passages are obtained based on BM25 and DPR respectively, and the union of them is reranked using BM25(q,p) + lambda*sim(q,p) as the ranking function. The value lambda = 1.1 was used, based on the retrieval accuracy in the development set.

query: How is autoregressivity preserved in a retrieval-augmented model that retrieves neighbours for the following chunk, and what happens at the positions where no neighbour can be attended to?
reference_answer: The last token of a chunk is the first to be able to access the retrieved content while maintaining autoregressivity. The first m-1 tokens cannot attend to any neighbour of a previous chunk, and at those positions chunked cross-attention is defined as the identity.

query: What changes were made to the standard GPT-style transformer to obtain the Retro baseline, and what baseline model sizes were trained?
reference_answer: The authors replace LayerNorm with RMSNorm and use relative position encodings. As baselines they train retrieval-free transformers with 132M, 368M, 1.3B and 7.0B parameters, with embedding matrices excluded from parameter counts.

query: By what mechanism do Borgeaud et al. (2022) argue a retrieval model could mitigate the privacy risk of having memorised its training data?
reference_answer: Retrieval models such as Retro that have access to the entire training dataset during inference exacerbate privacy issues by being able to directly copy training data, but retrieval systems offer a path towards mitigating these concerns via obliteration of the retrievable data at inference time.

query: How is language-modelling performance measured for the Retro models, and how is boundary contamination controlled when evaluating?
reference_answer: Bits-per-byte is used rather than loss because it is tokenizer agnostic. Evaluation uses a sequence length of 2048 tokens but a stride of 1024 within documents to mitigate boundary effects; a separate set of manually selected Wikipedia articles edited in September 2021 is also evaluated, months after the pre-training and retrieval data was collected.

query: How does scaling the retrieval database at evaluation time affect Retro, and over what range does the retrieval neighbour count help?
reference_answer: Scaling the retrieval database at evaluation improves language modelling performance dramatically, with gains as the retrieval data is increased from Wikipedia (4 billion tokens) to all of MassiveText (1.7T tokens). The smallest model improves with up to 10 neighbours whereas the 7B model improves with up to 40 neighbours.

query: What does retrieval add to the cost of sampling from a Retro model, compared with an ordinary transformer?
reference_answer: The cost of sampling is quadratic in the size of the sampled sequence, as when sampling from regular Transformers, while the added cost of retrieval is linear in the number of chunks and is negligible compared to the token sampling cost in practice.

query: What is the MSMARCO abstractive question answering task used by Lewis et al. (2020), and which of its resources are actually used?
reference_answer: The MSMARCO NLG task v2.1 is used. The task consists of questions, ten gold passages retrieved from a search engine for each question, and a full sentence answer annotated from the retrieved passages, but the supplied passages are not used, only the questions and answers.

query: In what sense can the RAG model of Lewis et al. (2020) be applied to a sequence classification task rather than to generation?
reference_answer: RAG can be used for sequence classification tasks by considering the target class as a target sequence of length one, in which case RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token are equivalent.

query: What does the per-token document posterior show about how RAG-Token assembles a Jeopardy answer from several retrieved documents?
reference_answer: When generating a book title such as Sun, the posterior is high for document 2 which mentions The Sun Also Rises, and document 1 dominates the posterior when A Farewell to Arms is generated. Jeopardy questions often contain two separate pieces of information, and RAG-Token may perform best because it can generate responses that combine content from several documents.

query: What is claimed to be gained by starting from pre-trained parametric and non-parametric components rather than training a retrieval mechanism from scratch?
reference_answer: In contrast to prior architectures trained from scratch for specific tasks, the setting explored uses pre-trained and pre-loaded parametric and non-parametric memory components, and crucially, by using pre-trained access mechanisms the ability to access knowledge is present without additional training.

query: How is generation diversity measured across the models compared by Lewis et al. (2020), and which RAG variant is reported as more diverse?
reference_answer: Generation diversity is investigated by calculating the ratio of distinct ngrams to total ngrams generated by the different models. Table 5 shows that RAG-Sequence's generations are more diverse than RAG-Token's, and that both are significantly more diverse than BART without needing any diversity-promoting decoding.

query: How does the number of documents retrieved at test time affect open-domain QA performance for each of the two RAG variants?
reference_answer: Retrieving more documents at test time monotonically improves open-domain QA results for RAG-Sequence, but performance peaks for RAG-Token at 10 retrieved documents.

query: Three of these systems retrieve passages and then generate an answer, but they treat the retrieved text differently once it comes back from the retriever. For each, state what is done to the passages between the retriever and the generator.
reference_answer: RAG leaves the passages untouched as evidence: to combine the input x with the retrieved content z when generating from BART, it simply concatenates them, so the retrieved text reaches the generator as plain concatenated context. Self-RAG puts the passages inside the model's own input and marks them: the retrieval special token =Yes is added and R retrieves the top K passages, and critique tokens are appended after the retrieved passage or generations. CRAG never passes the raw passages through at all: given a retrieved relevant document, a decompose-then-recompose knowledge refinement method is designed to further extract the most critical knowledge strips in it, and to obtain fine-grained retrieval results the retrieved results are segmented into internal strips.

query: Each of these systems retrieves from an external collection rather than from its own parameters, and each says something different about what that collection is. For each, state what the retrieved corpus is, what it is made of, and the dated snapshot or token count the paper gives for it.
reference_answer: RAG uses a single Wikipedia dump for all experiments as its non-parametric knowledge source and dates it: following Lee et al. and Karpukhin et al. it uses the December 2018 dump. REALM's knowledge corpus is derived from the December 20, 2018 snapshot of English Wikipedia, and it reports that the method of pre-training can be applied on two choices of the pre-training corpus: (1) Wikipedia, which is identical to the knowledge corpus, and (2) CC-News, its reproduction of the corpus of English news proposed by Liu et al. (2019). Retro uses a multi-lingual version of MassiveText for both training and retrieval data, a collection of text documents from multiple sources and multiple languages totalling over 5 trillion tokens, and during training it retrieves from 600B tokens from the training data.

query: Three of these pipelines retrieve with a retriever and differ in where that retriever came from and in whether the pipeline trains it. For each, state the retriever it starts from and whether that retriever receives any training from the pipeline itself.
reference_answer: Contriever is the retriever that is itself trained: all of its models are pre-trained on English Wikipedia for 200k gradient steps, the paper contrasts the two contrastive pre-training methods MoCo and in-batch negatives, and fine-tuning on MS MARCO takes 20k gradient steps with a batch size of 512. The paper positions this against BM25, which does not require supervision, and against supervised bi-encoders such as DPR and ANCE, which are trained on supervised data such as NaturalQuestions or MS MARCO. RAG starts from a pre-trained bi-encoder from DPR, which was trained to retrieve documents which contain answers to TriviaQA questions and Natural Questions, and then does train it: it jointly trains the retriever and generator components without any direct supervision on what document should be retrieved. Self-RAG trains no retriever at all: for the retriever model R it uses off-the-shelf Contriever-MS MARCO by default and retrieves up to ten documents for each input, i.e. the supervised MS MARCO fine-tuned version of the unsupervised contrastive model.
